title: Two fiduciae: refuge-adherence (essence of living faith) versus sense-assurance (fruit, not always felt)
source_text: XXIV. Plurimi quidem Theologi docent fiduciam in Deum per Christum esse ipsum formalem & specificum actum fidei vivae & justificantis. Verum observant Viri docti duplicem esse fiduciam. Unam quam vocant perfugii, atque adhaerentiae, qua fidelis Deo adhaeret, & in Christo salutem & justitiam quaerit, quae fiducia in Scriptura voce בטח & חסה exprimi solet. Alteram quam dicunt fiduciam sensus; qua quis de justitia & salute jam impetrata confidit, & ad Deum accedit absque timore atque formidine. Quae fiducia Hebraica voce מבטח significatur, & in Novo Testamento παρρησία & πεποίθησις dicitur. Prior illa pertinet ad essentiam fidei vivae & justificantis, & justificationis nostrae instrumentum est; seu conditio sine qua nemo justificatur. Altera vero est fidei fructus, sive effectus, quem perpetuo non exercent; quique non semper apparet & sentitur in fidelibus & justificatis, & unde non pendet necessario salus & justificatio. Petrus Molinaeus, Petri Molinaei filius, Tract. Gallico de Fide Justificante.
pass_a_gloss: Many theologians indeed teach that trust in God through Christ is itself the formal and specific act of living and justifying faith. But learned men observe that there is a twofold trust. One they call of refuge and adherence, by which the believer adheres to God and seeks salvation and righteousness in Christ—commonly expressed in Scripture by the Hebrew words for trusting and taking refuge. The other they call trust of sense, by which one confides concerning righteousness and salvation already obtained and approaches God without fear and dread—signified by another Hebrew term and in the New Testament called boldness and confidence. The former belongs to the essence of living and justifying faith and is the instrument or condition of our justification without which no one is justified. The latter is a fruit or effect of faith which they do not always exercise; which does not always appear and is felt in the justified, and on which salvation and justification do not necessarily depend. So Peter Du Moulin the son in his French treatise on justifying faith.
pass_b_english: Learned Reformed distinguish refuge-trust (faith’s essence and instrument) from sense-assurance (a fruit not always felt).
Salvation does not necessarily hang on the felt persuasion of already-obtained pardon.
